Text: Disney is planning a broad restructuring of its television business that could result in hundreds of job cuts and consolidate divisions that have operated separately, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The plan is being led by Debra OConnell, who oversees ABC Entertainment, 20th Television, Hulu Originals, Disney Kids & Family, National Geographic Content and Freeform. Disney Entertainment Television chief Dana Walden said the company plans to centralize the divisions into a single television business rather than separate silos. Text: Disney knows that business, like football, is a contact sport. Sometimes the hits come in-house from feuding among executives. Sometimes they come in court, from battling the Federal Communications Commission. And sometimes, Disney, which owns ABC, takes hits from its own affiliates. ABC station owners are irritated with Disney’s recent decision to air the Super Bowl on many different platforms, including Disney+, ESPN2, NFL Network and ESPNU. The game is already airing on both ABC and ESPN. The aggregate of the different platforms may drop advertising revenue associated with broadcast viewership by up to 35% compared to last year, according to a station group CEO who asked not to be named because the data is private. $DIS

Author: topstockalerts
Text: Disney has the broadcast rights to this season’s Super Bowl. ABC hasn’t had the Super Bowl since 2006. Disney got back in the Super Bowl rotation when it struck its most recent media rights deal with the NFL in 2021. The Super Bowl is a major moneymaker for ABC stations. Some of these are owned by Disney, but the vast majority are part of local station groups owned by companies such as Sinclair, Nexstar and Tegna. Fox said last year that Super Bowl ads generated more than $800 million in gross revenue across all platforms. The math for the main broadcast network is simple. There are about 85 30-second spots during a standard game. At $8 million a pop on average, that’s $680 million. $DIS

Author: topstockalerts
Text: Local affiliate stations pay the owners of the broadcast networks — Disney for ABC, Comcast for NBC, Fox for Fox and Skydance for CBS — a so-called reverse retransmission fee for the right to carry network programming. There’s a standard process to retransmission fee discussions. Disney pays billions for live sports and then asks its affiliates for money to help pay for them. The affiliates then negotiate with the pay-TV providers and charge them retrans fees. This is why the broadcast affiliates are steaming. For decades, the Super Bowl was exclusive to broadcast TV. Getting access to the Big Game was a big part of that fee. For years, media companies have made the Super Bowl available for both broadcast and streaming audiences. Still, this year, Disney has taken a wrecking ball to the broadcast exclusivity of the past. $DIS

Text: Walt Disney is planning a major overhaul of Disney+, introducing creator-led programming, short-form vertical video and a potential free ad-supported tier to compete more directly with social media platforms and expand user engagement. According to an internal presentation reported by Business Insider, the strategy is part of CEO Josh D’Amaro’s fiscal 2027 priorities, aimed at increasing time spent on the platform, attracting younger audiences and expanding advertising opportunities. Disney faces growing competition for viewing time. Nielsen data for August showed Disney’s streaming portfolio captured 4.8% of total U.S. TV viewing, ahead of Peacock and Paramount+, but behind Netflix at 7.7% and YouTube at 15.8%. The potential free tier could attract new users and generate additional advertising revenue, while creator content and vertical video would bring Disney+ closer to the formats popularized by social platforms. $DIS
